newsitem.title: KUWAIT: Oil prices could drop by end of 1997 - BP analyst.
newsitem.headline: Oil prices could drop by end of 1997 - BP analyst.

text.p: The price of North Sea Brent Blend crude oil could drop to $18 per barrel by the end of next year, British Petroleum Co Plc's chief economist said on Tuesday.
Peter Davies told a BP seminar in Kuwait that forward oil markets were assuming the price "will fall back fairly quickly and decline to $18 a barrel by the end of next year.
"This reflects the consensus by most forecasters...".
Brent crude oil futures for December delivery were trading just below $23 in London on Tuesday.

Davies said, with world benchmark Brent in 1996 likely to exceed earlier expectations and average around $20 for the year, $3 higher than the average for 1995, there were two views on what the price will do in 1997.

While some analysts expect a surplus of crude on the market over the next few months -- during the northern hemisphere winter -- others forecast some "tightness" with a normal winter and Iraqi oil exports still blocked.
"The Iraqi factor is important," he said.
Many market analysts had expected Baghdad's return to world markets with 700,000 barrels per day in September for the first time since its 1990 invasion of Kuwait.

Iraq's accord with the United Nations in May for limited oil sales worth $2 billion over a renewable six month period was halted when Baghdad sent troops into northern Iraq in August to help one Kurdish faction to fight against another.

Davies, who had not forecast the current rise in oil prices, said "nothing has changed from 1995...There were no fundamental differences" in 1996 to warrant the price increase or have a long-term impact.
He also said the added revenue from higher prices was not expected to trigger a change in exploration policy by oil majors, including BP, which "will not change policy on (price) fluctuations."
The price rise was offset by lower refining margins and petrochemical prices, he added.

Davies presented a study which said "The world is well supplied with proven energy resources...(which) increased and is currently at or extremely close to all time high levels. Discoveries and reserve additions continue to exceed consumption."
The International Energy Agency (IEA) last Friday said global oil demand will rise to 73.8 million bpd in the fourth quarter 1996, up 1.9 million year-on-year.

But supply should easily keep pace with demand, the IEA said, at an estimated 73.7 million bpd which includes a 1.8 million bpd increase in supplies from producers outside the Organisation of the Petroleum Exporting Countries (OPEC).
